question.stem: A company reports a $14,000 unrealized gain on an available-for-sale debt security, a $6,000 unrealized gain on a trading security, a $5,000 realized loss on an equipment sale, and $2,000 of dividend income. What pretax amount should the company report in other comprehensive income?

error_model.name: Include trading gain
error_model.misconception: Treats every unrealized security gain as OCI.

error_model.name: Net realized loss
error_model.misconception: Nets an earnings loss against OCI.

error_model.name: Include dividend income
error_model.misconception: Treats ordinary dividend income as OCI.

facts.statement: The unrealized gain on available-for-sale debt is $14,000.

facts.irrelevance_reason: Trading-security changes are reported in earnings.
A realized disposal loss is reported in earnings.
Ordinary dividend income is reported in earnings.

solution.end_ask: Identify and total the stated pretax OCI components.

representation.setup: Pretax OCI = included OCI items; exclude items reported in net income.

steps.instruction: Classify each item as OCI or earnings.
steps.result: Only the available-for-sale debt unrealized gain is OCI.

solution.keyed_answer_rationale: Only the $14,000 unrealized gain on available-for-sale debt is a current-period OCI item.
solution.faster_or_safer_route: First eliminate the three items explicitly reported in earnings; the remaining amount is OCI.

content.title: Pretax other comprehensive income components
content.rule_statement: Unrealized holding gains and losses on available-for-sale debt securities are excluded from earnings and reported in other comprehensive income, while trading-security changes, realized disposal results, and ordinary dividends are included in net income rather than OCI.
content.applicability: For-profit entities applying U.S. GAAP to the stated pretax security and income items.

assertions.claim: An unrealized holding gain on an available-for-sale debt security is reported in OCI before tax.
Trading-security gains, realized disposal losses, and dividend income are earnings items, not current-period OCI components.

question.stem: A company using the indirect method reports net income of $120,000, depreciation expense of $25,000, a gain on sale of equipment of $8,000, an $18,000 increase in accounts receivable, a $7,000 decrease in inventory, a $6,000 increase in accounts payable, and $10,000 of cash dividends paid. All stated working-capital changes relate to operations. What amount should the company report as net cash provided by operating activities?

error_model.name: Omit receivable increase
error_model.misconception: Fails to subtract the operating-asset increase.

error_model.name: Add sale gain
error_model.misconception: Adds rather than subtracts a gain already included in net income.

error_model.name: Subtract financing dividend
error_model.misconception: Treats dividends paid as an operating adjustment.

facts.use_in_solution: Starting point for the indirect reconciliation.
Added back as a noncash expense.
Subtracted because the gain is included in net income.

facts.irrelevance_reason: Dividends paid are a financing cash flow.

assumptions.statement: All stated working-capital changes relate to operating activities.

solution.end_ask: Reconcile net income to net cash provided by operating activities.

representation.setup: CFO = net income + noncash expenses - disposal gains - operating-asset increases + operating-asset decreases + operating-liability increases.

steps.instruction: Separate operating reconciliation items from the financing dividend.
Assign each operating adjustment its indirect-method sign.
steps.result: Add depreciation, inventory decrease, and payables increase; subtract the gain and receivables increase.

steps.instruction: Apply the signed adjustments to net income.

solution.keyed_answer_rationale: The correctly signed operating adjustments reconcile net income to $132,000; dividends paid stay in financing.
solution.faster_or_safer_route: Mark each change with a plus or minus before doing arithmetic, and cross out the financing dividend.

correctness_evidence.independence_limit: The generic checker recomputes the keyed amount solely from structured facts and coefficients; human review still owns accounting correctness, fairness, and learner readiness.

content.title: Indirect-method operating cash flow reconciliation
content.rule_statement: Under the indirect method, net income is adjusted for noncash items, gains or losses whose cash effects belong outside operating activities, and changes in operating assets and liabilities; dividends paid are financing cash flows.
content.applicability: For-profit entity statement of cash flows using the indirect method.

assertions.claim: Add depreciation and operating-liability increases, subtract disposal gains and operating-asset increases, and add operating-asset decreases in reconciling net income to operating cash flow.
Cash dividends paid are financing cash outflows and do not adjust operating cash flow.

question.stem: At year-end, a company has $40,000 in an unrestricted checking account. It also holds a $25,000 Treasury bill acquired with 76 days to maturity, a $30,000 Treasury note acquired with 106 days to maturity, and $15,000 of commercial paper acquired with 95 days to maturity. All three investments are highly liquid and readily convertible to known cash; the Treasury note pays 5% interest. What total should the company report as cash and cash equivalents?

error_model.name: Include Treasury note
error_model.misconception: Uses short remaining maturity at year-end instead of original maturity to the holder.

error_model.name: Include commercial paper
error_model.misconception: Treats a 95-day original maturity as within three months.

error_model.name: Exclude all investments
error_model.misconception: Treats cash equivalents as cash deposits only.

facts.use_in_solution: Included because its original maturity to the holder is within three months.

facts.statement: The Treasury bill had 76 days to maturity when acquired.
facts.use_in_solution: Establishes that the bill meets the original-maturity convention.

facts.irrelevance_reason: Its original maturity to the holder exceeds three months.

facts.statement: The Treasury note had 106 days to maturity when acquired.
facts.irrelevance_reason: This exceeds the generally three-month original-maturity convention.
Its original maturity to the holder exceeds three months.

facts.statement: The commercial paper had 95 days to maturity when acquired.
facts.irrelevance_reason: This exceeds the generally three-month original-maturity convention.

facts.statement: The Treasury note interest rate is 5%.
facts.irrelevance_reason: The coupon rate does not replace the stated original-maturity test.

assumptions.statement: All three investments are highly liquid and readily convertible to known amounts of cash.

solution.end_ask: Calculate the cash and cash equivalents total using original maturity to the holder.

representation.setup: Cash and cash equivalents = unrestricted cash + qualifying investments acquired with three months or less to maturity.

steps.instruction: Classify each investment using maturity at acquisition.
steps.result: Only the 76-day Treasury bill qualifies; 106 days and 95 days exceed the convention, and the coupon rate is not decisive.

solution.keyed_answer_rationale: The checking deposit and 76-day Treasury bill qualify; the other investments exceed three months at acquisition.
solution.faster_or_safer_route: Circle the acquisition-to-maturity days first; ignore the coupon rate and eliminate investments over three months.

blueprint.mcq_scope_limit: The MCQ tests a bounded maturity classification and not all restrictions, overdrafts, or presentation issues.

content.title: Cash-equivalent original-maturity convention
content.rule_statement: Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible to known cash and so near maturity that interest-rate risk is insignificant; generally only investments with an original maturity to the holder of three months or less qualify.
content.applicability: For-profit entity classifying highly liquid investments as cash equivalents under U.S. GAAP.

assertions.claim: Apply the generally three-month-or-less test from the acquisition date to maturity, not from the reporting date.
Unrestricted checking deposits are cash and are included with qualifying cash equivalents.

question.stem: An inventory analyst is reconciling records that show beginning inventory of $180,000, purchases received of $520,000, cost of goods sold of $470,000, returns to suppliers of $20,000, and a supported physical count of $205,000. Sales revenue was $700,000. All inventory amounts are at cost, no write-down is indicated, and the source records are complete. What adjustment should be made to the inventory general ledger?

error_model.name: Reverse adjustment direction
error_model.misconception: Computes book minus physical instead of the adjustment needed to move book to physical.

error_model.name: Assume records agree
error_model.misconception: Stops after accepting the physical count without comparing it to the rollforward.

error_model.name: Omit supplier returns
error_model.misconception: Leaves returned goods in the book rollforward.

facts.use_in_solution: Subtracted from purchases in the rollforward.

facts.irrelevance_reason: Revenue does not enter this cost-basis inventory rollforward.

assumptions.statement: The stated source records are complete and the physical count is supported.
All inventory amounts are measured at cost and no lower-measurement adjustment is indicated.

solution.end_ask: Determine the signed adjustment that moves book inventory to the supported physical amount.

representation.setup: Book ending inventory = beginning + purchases - COGS - supplier returns; adjustment = physical - book.

steps.instruction: Compare supported physical inventory with the book balance.
Translate the signed difference into the ledger action.

solution.keyed_answer_rationale: Book inventory is $210,000 and supported physical inventory is $205,000, so the ledger must decrease $5,000.
solution.faster_or_safer_route: Write the rollforward signs before calculating, then use target minus book to preserve adjustment direction.

content.title: Inventory cost rollforward and physical reconciliation
content.rule_statement: Inventory is measured on a cost basis subject to applicable subsequent-measurement rules; a cost rollforward adds inventory purchases and subtracts cost assigned to goods sold and supplier returns, and the resulting book balance is reconciled to inventory on hand.
content.applicability: For-profit entity inventory carried at cost where no lower-measurement adjustment is stated.

assertions.claim: Ending book inventory equals beginning inventory plus purchases minus cost of goods sold minus returns to suppliers for the stated fact pattern.
The general-ledger balance is adjusted to the supported physical inventory amount when the difference is valid and no other reconciling item remains.

question.stem: A company concludes that a litigation loss is probable and estimates the loss between $300,000 and $500,000, with no amount in the range a better estimate than another. A separate claim has a reasonably possible loss of $200,000. What total loss should the company accrue?

error_model.name: Accrue maximum
error_model.misconception: Uses conservatism to select the high end despite no better estimate.

error_model.name: Accrue midpoint
error_model.misconception: Averages the endpoints without evidence that the midpoint is a better estimate.

error_model.name: Accrue possible claim
error_model.misconception: Adds a merely reasonably possible claim to the probable range maximum.

facts.statement: The probable loss range minimum is $300,000.
facts.use_in_solution: Accrued because no point is a better estimate.

facts.statement: The probable loss range maximum is $500,000.
facts.irrelevance_reason: The maximum is not accrued when no point is a better estimate.

facts.statement: The separate reasonably possible loss is $200,000.
facts.irrelevance_reason: A reasonably possible loss is not accrued under the stated facts.

solution.end_ask: Calculate the amount accrued for the stated loss contingencies.

representation.setup: Accrual = minimum of probable estimable range when no point is better; exclude reasonably possible claim.

steps.instruction: Select the measurement rule for the probable range.
steps.result: Use the $300,000 minimum because no amount is a better estimate.

steps.instruction: Apply the likelihood threshold to the separate claim.
steps.result: Exclude the $200,000 reasonably possible loss from accrual.

solution.keyed_answer_rationale: The minimum of the probable range is accrued, and the separate reasonably possible claim is not accrued.
solution.faster_or_safer_route: Underline 'no amount is a better estimate' and 'reasonably possible'; those phrases determine the minimum and exclusion without averaging.

correctness_evidence.independence_limit: The generic checker recomputes the keyed amount solely from structured facts and coefficients; human review still owns accounting correctness, fairness, and learner readiness.

blueprint.mcq_scope_limit: The MCQ calculates one accrual and does not draft the full journal entry or disclosures.

content.title: Loss contingency range measurement
content.rule_statement: When a probable loss is reasonably estimable as a range and no amount within the range is a better estimate than another, the minimum amount in the range is accrued; a merely reasonably possible separate loss is not accrued.
content.applicability: For-profit entity loss contingencies under U.S. GAAP with the stated likelihood and estimability conclusions.

assertions.claim: Accrue the minimum of a probable loss range when no point in the range is a better estimate.
Do not accrue a separate loss assessed as reasonably possible rather than probable.

question.stem: Before issuing its year-end financial statements, a company learns that a customer owing $90,000 entered bankruptcy because of severe financial difficulty already present at year-end; no credit loss has yet been recorded for that receivable. A warehouse with a carrying amount of $400,000 was destroyed by a fire that began after year-end. The company also settles a year-end lawsuit for $60,000 after having accrued $35,000. After distinguishing adjustment from disclosure, what total additional loss should the company recognize in its year-end financial statements?

error_model.misconception: Adjusts for the post-year-end fire but overlooks the lawsuit increment.

error_model.name: Recognize all events
error_model.misconception: Includes the nonrecognized fire along with both recognized adjustments.

error_model.name: Ignore prior lawsuit accrual
error_model.misconception: Adds the full settlement rather than only the increment over the existing accrual.

solution.end_ask: Total only the additional year-end losses supported by recognized subsequent events.

representation.setup: Additional loss = confirmed year-end receivable loss + (lawsuit settlement - existing accrual); exclude post-year-end fire from recognition.

steps.instruction: Classify each event by when its underlying condition arose.
steps.result: Recognize the bankruptcy evidence and lawsuit update; do not recognize the later-arising fire in the year-end amounts.

solution.keyed_answer_rationale: The bankruptcy confirms a year-end loss of $90,000 and the lawsuit needs another $25,000; the later-arising fire is not recognized.
solution.faster_or_safer_route: Draw a year-end line: put pre-existing conditions on the adjustment side, later-arising conditions on the disclosure-only side, then subtract any amount already accrued.

labels.task: Derive the impact to the financial statements and required note disclosures due to identified subsequent events.

content.title: Recognized and nonrecognized subsequent events
content.rule_statement: A subsequent event is recognized when it provides additional evidence about conditions existing at the balance-sheet date; an event evidencing conditions arising after that date is not recognized in those statements, although material nonrecognized events may require disclosure.
content.applicability: For-profit entity evaluating events after year-end but before financial statements are issued.

assertions.claim: Recognize the effects of subsequent evidence about a condition that existed at the balance-sheet date.
Do not adjust for a condition arising after the balance-sheet date; disclose it if material under the applicable requirements.
